items.prompt: Which habit helps to keep your teeth healthy?

options.text: eating sweets just before bed
options.why: Sugar left on teeth overnight feeds bacteria that make acid, and acid can make holes in teeth.

options.text: brushing your teeth twice a day
brushing your teeth once a week
options.why: Once a week is not enough. Brush in the morning and before bed.

options.text: sipping sugary drinks all day
options.why: Sugary drinks cover your teeth in sugar again and again.

hints: Think about what removes food and sugar from your teeth.
Bacteria in your mouth use sugar to make acid, and acid damages teeth.
Cross out the choices that leave sugar on your teeth for a long time.
items.explanation: Brushing in the morning and before bed removes food and bacteria from your teeth. This stops acid building up and making holes in them.

items.prompt: Match each food group to its main job in the body.
pairs: help the body grow and repair itself
help keep the body working well
helps food move through the gut
hints: Each food group has one main job. Think about running, growing and staying well.
Think of an example food for each group, such as rice, eggs, fruit or vegetables.
Start with carbohydrates. Rice and bread give you the power to run and play.
items.explanation: Carbohydrates such as rice give energy, and proteins such as eggs help the body grow and repair. Vitamins and minerals keep the body working well, and fibre helps food move through the gut.

items.prompt: Which food is rich in protein?

options.text: rice
options.why: Rice is mostly carbohydrate, which gives energy.

options.text: mango
options.why: Mangoes give vitamins, fibre and natural sugars, with very little protein.

options.text: cooking oil
options.why: Cooking oil is a fat. It stores energy but has no protein.

options.text: tempeh

hints: Protein helps the body grow and repair itself.
Protein foods often come from animals, beans or soya beans.
Cross out the fruit and the oil first. Then compare the two foods that are left.
items.explanation: Tempeh is made from soya beans, which are rich in protein. Rice is mostly carbohydrate, mango gives vitamins and oil is a fat.

items.prompt: Sort the foods by the main food group in each one.
hints: Carbohydrates give quick energy, proteins help you grow and fats store energy.
Think about where each food comes from: grains and roots, animals and beans, or oils.
Start with the foods made from grains or roots, such as rice.
items.explanation: Rice, bread and sweet potato are mostly carbohydrate. Fish, tofu and chicken are rich in protein, while butter and cooking oil are fats.

items.prompt: Choose all the habits that help to stop harmful microorganisms spreading.

options.text: washing your hands with soap before eating
covering your mouth when you cough or sneeze
sharing a drinking bottle with a friend who is ill
options.why: Microorganisms from the ill person can pass to you on the bottle.

options.text: keeping food covered so flies cannot land on it
rinsing your hands with cold water only
options.why: Water alone leaves many microorganisms behind. Soap removes far more.

hints: Harmful microorganisms spread on hands, in droplets from coughs and on flies.
For each habit, ask whether it stops microorganisms reaching your mouth or someone else.
Start with the habits that use soap or a cover. Then think about sharing and rinsing.
items.explanation: Soap, covering coughs and covering food all stop microorganisms reaching people. Sharing a bottle with someone who is ill, or rinsing without soap, lets microorganisms spread.

items.prompt: Which food is made with the help of useful microorganisms?

options.text: boiled rice
options.why: Rice is cooked with heat in water. No microorganism is needed.

options.text: orange juice
options.why: Juice is squeezed from fruit. No microorganism is needed.

options.text: tapai, made from cassava
sea salt
options.why: Sea salt is left behind when sea water evaporates. No microorganism is needed.

hints: Some foods change because tiny living things grow in them for a few days.
Yeast is a useful microorganism. It can make food soft, sweet or bubbly.
Cross out the foods that are only cooked, squeezed or dried.
items.explanation: Tapai is made by adding ragi to cooked cassava. Ragi contains yeasts and moulds, useful microorganisms that turn the starch into sugars and make the cassava sweet and soft.

items.prompt: Look at the table. Which lunch box gives the most balanced meal?

figure.caption: What is in each lunch box
head: Lunch box
Foods inside
figure.alt: Table of four lunch boxes. A: rice, fried chicken and cake. B: rice, fish, spinach and papaya. C: bread, jam and sweet biscuits. D: noodles, rice and crackers.

options.text: Box A
options.why: Box A has carbohydrate and protein, but no fruit or vegetables.

options.text: Box B
Box C
options.why: Box C is mostly carbohydrate and sugar, with no protein, fruit or vegetables.

options.text: Box D
options.why: Box D has three carbohydrate foods and nothing from the other groups.

hints: A balanced meal has foods from several different food groups.
Look for a carbohydrate, a protein, and a fruit or vegetable in the same box.
Check each box for a vegetable or a fruit first.
items.explanation: Box B has carbohydrate (rice), protein (fish), and vitamins, minerals and fibre (spinach and papaya). Eating from several food groups gives the body what it needs.

items.prompt: Plan a balanced lunch for a school day. Name four foods and say which food group each one belongs to. Explain why your lunch is balanced.

criteria.label: Gives a correct food group for each food
Includes a fruit or a vegetable
Explains why the meal is balanced

planning: Which food will give you energy?
Which food will help you grow?
Which fruit or vegetable will you add?
items.model: For lunch I will have brown rice, which is a carbohydrate that gives me energy. I will add grilled fish for protein to help me grow. I will also eat stir-fried kangkung and a slice of watermelon for vitamins, minerals and fibre. My lunch is balanced because it has food from several food groups.
hints: Start with a food that gives you energy.
Add one food for growing and one fruit or vegetable.
items.explanation: A balanced lunch includes a carbohydrate for energy, a protein for growth and repair, and fruit or vegetables for vitamins, minerals and fibre.

items.prompt: In 1796, Edward Jenner tested an idea that led to the first vaccine. What does a vaccine do?

options.text: It cures every illness straight away.
options.why: A vaccine protects against one particular disease. It does not cure every illness.

options.text: It kills microorganisms on your hands.
options.why: Soap and water do that. A vaccine works inside the body.

options.text: It gives the body extra vitamins.
options.why: Vitamins come from food. A vaccine trains the body's defences.

options.text: It helps the body learn to fight a disease before you catch it.

hints: Jenner wanted to stop people from catching a disease in the first place.
Think about the difference between preventing a disease and curing it.
Cross out the choices about soap and food first.
items.explanation: A vaccine trains the body's defences to recognise a disease, so the body can fight it quickly later. Jenner's 1796 test against smallpox led to the first vaccine.

items.prompt: Class 5A washes their hands with water only. Class 5B uses soap and water. Each class touches a slice of bread, and both slices are sealed in bags for five days. Which result is most likely?

options.text: Both slices grow the same amount of mould.
options.why: Soap removes more microorganisms, so fewer reach the bread from Class 5B.

options.text: The bread from Class 5B grows less mould.
The bread from Class 5A grows no mould at all.
options.why: Water alone leaves many microorganisms on hands, so mould can still grow.

options.text: Mould only grows on bread kept in a fridge.
options.why: Mould grows faster in warm places than in a cold fridge.

hints: Mould and bacteria grow from microorganisms that land on the bread.
Think about which hands carried more microorganisms onto the bread.
Compare water only with soap and water. Decide which removes more microorganisms.
items.explanation: Soap and water remove more microorganisms than water alone. Fewer microorganisms reach Class 5B's bread, so less mould grows on it.

items.prompt: Which activity helps to keep your heart strong?

options.text: Sitting still for most of the day
options.why: A heart is a muscle and needs exercise to stay strong.

options.text: Sleeping with the lights on
options.why: Sleep is good for you, but it does not exercise the heart.

options.text: Running and playing games outside
Eating a big meal
options.why: A meal gives you energy, but the heart still needs exercise.

hints: Your heart is a muscle.
Muscles get stronger when they are used.
Choose the activity that makes your heart beat faster.
items.explanation: Hard exercise makes the heart work harder, and regular exercise keeps the heart muscle strong.

items.prompt: Sort the habits into those that help your health and those that can harm it.

items.text: Washing hands with soap before meals
Staying up very late on school nights
Never washing hands after the toilet

hints: Ask: does this habit protect my body or put it at risk?
Think about teeth, germs and sleep.
Start with the habits you already do at school.
items.explanation: Hand washing, tooth brushing and exercise protect your health. Too much sugar, too little sleep and unwashed hands can cause problems.

items.prompt: Dewi records the cups of water she drinks. Complete the table.
head: Day
Cups of water
hints: Add the five daily amounts.
Add in pairs that make easy numbers.
4 + 6 = 10 is a good first step.

items.prompt: Four children record the minutes they exercised yesterday. Who exercised for exactly twice as long as Bayu?

figure.alt: Bar chart of minutes of exercise: Bayu 20, Putri 30, Leo 40, Maya 60.

options.text: Leo
Putri
options.why: Putri exercised for 30 minutes, which is one and a half times as long as Bayu.

options.text: Maya
options.why: Maya exercised for three times as long as Bayu, not twice.

options.text: Nobody
options.why: Look again: one child did exactly double.

hints: Read Bayu's bar first.
Double means multiply by 2.
Find the bar that is twice as tall as Bayu's bar.
items.explanation: Bayu exercised for 20 minutes. Twice as long is 40 minutes, which is Leo.

items.prompt: Choose all the ways that harmful microorganisms can spread from one person to another.

options.text: Sneezing without covering your nose
Sharing a cup with a friend who is ill
Eating with hands that have touched a dirty surface
Washing fruit before you eat it
Keeping food in a clean cupboard

hints: Think about how tiny living things move from one place to another.
Two of the choices are ways of staying safe.
Check each one: could it carry germs to someone?
items.explanation: Sneezes, shared cups and dirty hands can pass on microorganisms. Washing fruit and keeping food clean help to stop them spreading.

items.prompt: Fish, beans and eggs give the body protein. Protein helps the body grow and ___ itself.
hints: Think about what happens when you have a small cut.
The word starts with r.
It means to fix damage.
items.explanation: Protein is the body-building nutrient. It helps the body to grow and to repair itself.

items.prompt: Match each food to the main nutrient it gives.
hints: Each food is mostly rich in one nutrient.
Think about what the food is made from.
Match the food that gives energy quickly, such as a grain food.
items.explanation: Bread is a source of carbohydrate, tempeh gives protein, butter is mostly fat and oranges are rich in vitamins.

items.prompt: Bread rises because ___ makes gas. Some microorganisms can make us ill, so we should wash our ___ with ___.
hints: One kind of microorganism helps bakers.
Think about which part of your body touches food.
Which choice would actually remove germs?
items.explanation: Yeast is a useful microorganism that makes bread rise. Washing hands with soap and water removes harmful ones.

items.prompt: Hadi keeps three slices of bread in different places for six days. What does the table show about temperature and mould?

head: Place
Day 2
Day 4
Day 6
figure.alt: Table of the percentage of each bread slice covered by mould. Warm cupboard: 5, 30, 80. Kitchen shelf: 0, 10, 35. Fridge: 0, 2, 8 on days 2, 4 and 6.

options.text: Bread in the fridge had no mould at all.
options.why: The fridge slice still had 8 percent of its surface covered by day 6.

options.text: Mould grew much more slowly in the cold fridge.
Mould grew fastest on the kitchen shelf.
options.why: The warm cupboard slice had the most mould.

options.text: Mould grew at the same rate in every place.
options.why: The amounts covered are very different on day 6.

hints: Compare the day 6 readings for the three places.
Cold, cool and warm are the three temperatures.
Look at which place has the smallest number on day 6.
items.explanation: The warm cupboard slice was 80 percent covered by day 6 but the fridge slice only 8 percent. Low temperature slows the growth of mould.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to show how too much sugar can lead to a hole in a tooth.
items: Bacteria in the mouth feed on sugar left on the teeth
The acid wears away the hard outer layer of the tooth
A hole called a cavity can form
hints: Start with the cause and finish with the result.
The bacteria need something to feed on first.
Sugar is the first step.
items.explanation: Bacteria feed on sugar and make acid. The acid wears away the tooth, and a cavity can form.

items.prompt: The table shows the hours of sleep five children had last night. What is the mean number of hours?

head: Child
Hours of sleep
figure.alt: Table of hours of sleep: Rangga 9, Citra 10, Joko 11, Sekar 8, Wulan 12.

hints: The mean is the total shared out equally.
Add all five numbers, then divide.
9 + 10 + 11 + 8 + 12 is the total.
items.explanation: The total is 50 hours. 50 shared between 5 children is 10 hours each.

items.prompt: Maya says that all microorganisms are harmful. Which fact shows that she is wrong?

options.text: Bacteria are used to make yoghurt.
Microorganisms are too small to see.
options.why: Being tiny does not show whether they are harmful or useful.

options.text: Some microorganisms cause colds.
options.why: This supports Maya instead of proving her wrong.

options.text: Soap helps to remove microorganisms from hands.
options.why: This tells you how to remove them but not whether all are harmful.

hints: You need a fact about microorganisms that are helpful.
Think about foods made using microorganisms.
Find the fact that gives a useful job to some microorganisms.
items.explanation: Some microorganisms are useful. Bacteria make yoghurt and yeast makes bread rise.

items.prompt: Two schools of the same size count children absent with colds each month. School A began hand washing before meals in month 3. School B changed nothing. What is the best conclusion?

head: Month
School A
School B
figure.alt: Table of children absent with colds. School A: 18, 20, 12, 7 in months 1 to 4. School B: 17, 19, 18, 20.

options.text: Hand washing stopped all colds at School A.
options.why: School A still had 7 absences in month 4, so colds were reduced and not stopped.

options.text: School B shows that hand washing makes colds worse.
options.why: School B did not wash hands more, so it tells us nothing about hand washing making things worse.

options.text: The results cannot show anything, because the schools are different.
options.why: School B acts as a comparison: it stayed about the same while School A fell.

options.text: Hand washing probably helped School A, because School B did not improve without it.

hints: Which school acts as the comparison, or control?
Look at what happened in each school before and after month 3.
Ask what School B would have looked like without any change.
items.explanation: Absences fell in School A after hand washing began, but stayed high in School B. This suggests hand washing helped, although it did not stop all colds.

items.prompt: Why does your body need water?

options.text: Water helps to carry things around the body and keeps it working.
Water gives you energy in the same way as sugar.
options.why: Water has no energy. Food gives energy.

options.text: Water builds new muscle.
options.why: Muscles are built from protein.

options.text: Water stops you needing sleep.
options.why: Water does not replace sleep.

hints: Think about what blood is mostly made of.
Your body loses water when you sweat and when you go to the toilet.
Choose the answer that says water helps the body work.
items.explanation: Every part of the body needs water. It helps carry nutrients in the blood and replaces water lost in sweat and urine.

items.prompt: Tap the food on the plate that is the best source of protein.

figure.alt: A round plate with three foods on it: a bowl of rice on the left, a carrot on the right and an egg at the top.

hints: Protein helps the body grow and repair.
Rice gives mostly energy and carrot gives vitamins.
Animal foods such as meat, fish and eggs are rich in protein.
items.explanation: Eggs are rich in protein. Rice is mainly carbohydrate and a carrot gives vitamins and fibre.
